column3: Tall forest of big trees growing along rivers on rich alluvial soil.
column4: Along the Okavango, Chobe, Khwai and Boteti rivers and on Delta islands.
column5: Gives shade, fruit and cover to elephant, bushbuck, leopard and many birds.
column6: Look for jackal berry, sausage tree, knob thorn and African mangosteen.
column7: Long daylight hours and constant water explain the forests along the Delta rivers.

column3: Woodland or scrub of mopane trees, from 2 m scrub to 30 m "cathedral mopane".
column4: Alluvial clay soils of northern Botswana, e.g. Chobe, Savuti and Moremi.
column5: Good habitat for elephant and buffalo; mopane worms feed on the leaves.
column6: Show the butterfly-shaped leaves; they fold together in the midday heat.
column7: Mopane scrub also holds russet bush-willow and shepherd's tree.

column3: Dry bush savanna growing on deep, nutrient-poor Kalahari sand.
column4: Most of central and southern Botswana, e.g. CKGR and Kgalagadi.
column5: Supports desert-adapted animals like gemsbok, springbok and red hartebeest.
column6: Look for deep-rooted camel thorn and Kalahari apple-leaf trees.
column7: Sand holds little water, so the grasses here are poor grazing (e.g. three-awn grass).

column3: Grassland dotted with thorn trees such as the umbrella thorn.
column4: Poorly drained alluvial soils on the edges of floodplains and pans.
column5: Thorn pods and leaves feed giraffe, kudu, impala and elephant.
column6: Many "acacias" are now called Vachellia or Senegalia in new books.
column7: The umbrella thorn grows well in the alluvial soils of floodplain savanna.

column3: Large open areas covered mainly by grass, with few or no trees.
column4: Nxai Pan, Savuti Marsh and the Makgadikgadi grasslands.
column5: Grazers such as zebra, wildebeest and springbok feed here, followed by predators.
column6: Open plains are good places to watch cheetah hunting.
column7: Habitats are usually named after their main plants, e.g. grassland.

column3: Grassy plains that flood each year when the Okavango water arrives.
column4: Seasonal swamps of the Okavango Delta, Khwai and Linyanti.
column5: Rich grazing for red lechwe, buffalo and zebra, and food for many water birds.
column6: The flood peaks in the dry winter months, long after the rains in Angola.
column7: Red lechwe have long hooves to run through shallow floodwater.

column3: Permanent swamp lined with tall papyrus sedge, up to about 5 m high.
column4: The Okavango Panhandle and the permanent channels of the Delta.
column5: Papyrus roots trap silt and help build the Delta; sitatunga hide in it.
column6: Look for sitatunga and listen for swamp boubou from a boat.
column7: The Delta drops only 60 m over 250 km, so channels wind slowly through papyrus.

column3: A deep, open, permanent pool of water in the Delta.
column4: Permanent swamp areas, e.g. Xakanaxa and Gcodikwe in Moremi.
column5: Home to hippo, crocodile and fish, and nesting sites for herons and storks.
column6: Never swim in lagoons and keep boats well away from hippo.
column7: Gcodikwe lagoon has one of the largest heronries in southern Africa.

column3: A Delta island that often starts as a termite mound and grows as trees take root.
column4: Thousands are scattered across the Okavango Delta floodplains.
column5: Gives dry ground for trees, nesting birds and animals during the flood.
column6: Point out the ring of trees and the bare, salty centre of older islands.
column7: Salts build up in island centres as water evaporates, until plants cannot grow.

column3: A flat, dry lake bed covered with a white salt crust.
column4: Makgadikgadi (Sua and Ntwetwe) and many small Kalahari pans.
column5: After good rains pans fill and flamingos come to breed.
column6: Never drive on a wet pan: vehicles sink through the crust.
column7: Makgadikgadi is what remains of the huge ancient Lake Makgadikgadi.

column3: Long, low ridges of red Kalahari sand, held in place by grass.
column4: South-western Botswana, especially the Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park.
column5: Home to gemsbok, springbok, meerkats and many burrowing animals.
column6: Read the tracks in the sand early in the morning.
column7: The red colour comes from iron oxide coating the sand grains.

column3: Herbivores (primary consumers) that feed mainly on grass.
column4: Grasslands, floodplains and open savanna.
column5: They turn grass into food for predators, scavengers and decomposers.
column6: Examples: zebra, buffalo, tsessebe and wildebeest.
column7: Some are bulk grazers (e.g. buffalo); others are selective grazers.

column3: Herbivores that eat leaves, fruit, seeds and twig tips of trees and shrubs.
column4: Woodland and bush savanna.
column5: Browse at many heights lets many species share the same trees.
column6: Examples: giraffe, kudu and eland; they seldom eat grass.
column7: Savanna has browse at many levels plus grazing, so it supports many species.

column3: A food chain: sun to plants to herbivores to predators to scavengers.
column4: Everywhere in the bush; easiest to show at a kill.
column5: Predators keep herbivore numbers healthy and in balance.
column6: Only about 10% of the energy passes up to the next level.
column7: Many food chains link together to form a food web.

column3: Animals that feed on dead animals or steal kills from predators.
column4: Seen at carcasses in all habitats.
column5: They clean up carcasses and help stop disease spreading.
column6: Circling or dropping vultures can lead you to a kill.
column7: Lions and leopards scavenge too, but they are not true scavengers.

column3: Fungi and bacteria that break down dead plants and animals.
column4: Dead wood, dung, leaf litter and termite mounds.
column5: They return nutrients to the soil so plants can grow again.
column6: Show guests fungi on dead logs as nature's recyclers.
column7: Decomposers are the essential link in the nutrient cycle.

column3: A detritivore beetle that feeds on and breeds in animal dung.
column4: Common near fresh dung, mostly in the rainy season.
column5: Buries dung, which feeds the soil and plants.
column6: Point out the rolled ball; females lay eggs inside buried balls.
column7: Dung beetles can use the sun and the Milky Way to roll in a straight line.

column3: A relationship where both partners benefit.
column4: Oxpeckers ride on buffalo, giraffe and other large mammals.
column5: Oxpeckers eat ticks, and the host gets rid of parasites.
column6: Other examples: honeyguide and honey badger; elephant and marula.
column7: Oxpeckers also feed on blood from wounds, so the benefit is sometimes debated.

column3: Elephants eat fruit such as marula and spread the seeds in their dung.
column4: Wherever elephants feed, especially in marula and palm woodland.
column5: Seeds land in a nitrogen-rich heap of manure, ready to grow.
column6: Break open old dung to show guests seeds and plant fibre.
column7: Elephants digest less than half of what they eat.

column3: A relationship where one partner benefits and the other is unaffected.
column4: Cattle egrets follow buffalo, lechwe and elephant in grassland.
column5: The grazers disturb insects, which the egrets catch.
column6: Other examples: hornbills nesting in tree holes; waxbills nesting by wasp nests.
column7: Cattle egrets also follow cattle and tractors.

column3: A relationship where the parasite benefits and the host is harmed.
column4: Mistletoe grows on many savanna trees, e.g. acacias.
column5: Mistletoe roots grow under the bark and take the host tree's sugars.
column6: Other examples: parasitic wasps in caterpillars; ticks on game.
column7: The sour plum is a partial parasite on the roots of grasses.

column3: Intra-specific competition: animals of one species compete for something scarce.
column4: Seen in impala herds during the rutting season.
column5: Only the strongest rams win mates and pass on their genes.
column6: Inter-specific competition is between species, e.g. kingfisher and starling for nest holes.
column7: Impala rams fight for dominance during the rut.

column3: Fire is a natural factor that shapes savanna and grassland.
column4: Grasslands and floodplains, mainly in the dry season.
column5: Helps some seeds germinate, controls invader plants and removes dead grass.
column6: Fires that are too frequent or at the wrong time harm many organisms.
column7: Fresh green grass after a burn quickly attracts grazers.

column3: The most animals an area can support for ever without damaging it.
column4: Easy to see along the Chobe riverfront and at Savuti.
column5: Too many elephants push over and debark trees, changing woodland to scrub.
column6: Water, temperature, sunlight, soils and fire all limit carrying capacity.
column7: Old, leached Kalahari sands give lower carrying capacity than East Africa.

column3: An intrusive igneous rock that cooled slowly underground, so it has large crystals.
column4: Granite hills and kopjes in eastern Botswana, e.g. around Francistown and the Tswapong area.
column5: Granite weathers into sandy, nutrient-poor soils; the Kalahari sand is of granitic origin.
column6: Look for a speckled rock of pink or white feldspar, glassy quartz and black mica crystals.
column7: Granite cooled so slowly deep underground that its crystals had time to grow big enough to see.

column3: A dark, fine-grained extrusive igneous rock formed when lava cools quickly at the surface.
column4: Under parts of eastern and northern Botswana; often hidden below Kalahari sand.
column5: Basalt weathers into dark, very fertile clay soils that support good grazing.
column6: Dark grey to black, heavy, with crystals too small to see; may form six-sided columns.
column7: Basalt weathers fast, which is why basalt soils are rich and support many game animals.

column3: A pale, fine-grained extrusive igneous rock from sticky, silica-rich lava.
column4: The Savuti Hills (Gubatsa Hills) in Chobe National Park are made of flow-banded rhyolite.
column5: Rocky hills like Savuti give shelter and lookouts for leopard, klipspringer and rock hyrax.
column6: Look for fine bands or swirls in the rock, left by lava that flowed before it set.
column7: The Savuti rhyolite hills are more than 900 million years old.

column3: A sedimentary rock made of sand grains cemented together.
column4: The Otse Hills in south-east Botswana are mainly sandstone.
column5: Sandstone weathers back into sand, giving light soils that drain quickly.
column6: Rub it: it feels gritty like sandpaper. Layers (bedding) are often visible.
column7: Slanting layers in sandstone show the direction of ancient wind or water currents.

column3: A fine-grained sedimentary rock formed from compacted clay or mud.
column4: Found under the sand in places; seen in road cuts and quarries rather than game areas.
column5: Under heat and pressure shale changes into slate and then schist.
column6: Grey, thin layers that split easily into flat flakes.
column7: Shale is the most common sedimentary rock on Earth.

column3: A sedimentary rock built from shells, corals and bones, made of calcium carbonate.
column4: The Gcwihaba, Aha and Koanaka hills in the far north-west contain limestone, marble and dolomite.
column5: Water with carbon dioxide dissolves limestone, forming caves such as Drotsky's Cave.
column6: Pale grey or white; a drop of acid (or vinegar) makes it fizz.
column7: Rocks of organic origin like limestone are not "true" rocks, says the manual.

column3: A sedimentary rock like limestone but rich in magnesium.
column4: The Gcwihaba, Aha and Koanaka hills near the Namibian border.
column5: Dolomite hills are good for cave formation, home to bats and the Gcwihaba Caves.
column6: Looks like grey limestone, often in layers, but fizzes only weakly with acid.
column7: Drotsky's Cave in the dolomite hills may be a million years old or more.

column3: A very hard metamorphic rock formed when sandstone is changed by heat and pressure.
column4: The Tsodilo Hills in north-west Botswana are made of quartzite.
column5: Quartzite resists weathering, so it stands up as hills above the flat Kalahari sand.
column6: Hard, glassy and often pink, purple or grey; it breaks through the grains, not around them.
column7: Tsodilo's quartzite cliffs are covered in over 4 000 San rock paintings.

column3: A metamorphic rock formed from shale under high heat and pressure.
column4: Found in the older rocks of eastern Botswana, but rarely seen in safari areas.
column5: It shows how one rock type can change into another in the rock cycle.
column6: Look for shiny flakes of mica in wavy layers; it glitters in the sun.
column7: The manual's table shows shale, basalt and slate can all change into schist.

column3: A mineral of pure carbon, the hardest natural substance, formed deep in the mantle.
column4: Mined at Orapa, Jwaneng, Letlhakane and Karowe; not seen in the wild.
column5: Diamonds are Botswana's main export and paid for much of the country's development.
column6: Rough diamonds look like greasy, eight-sided crystals, not sparkly cut gems.
column7: Diamond is one of the few "rocks" made of a single mineral, with gold, silver and platinum.

column3: A dark igneous rock from deep in the mantle that can carry diamonds to the surface.
column4: Kimberlite pipes lie under the Kalahari sand at Orapa, Jwaneng and Letlhakane.
column5: All of Botswana's diamonds are mined from kimberlite pipes.
column6: Greenish-grey to blue-grey rock with scattered rounded crystals and bits of other rock.
column7: Orapa, found in 1967, is one of the largest kimberlite pipes in the world.

column3: A hard, pale layer of sand and gravel cemented by lime (calcium carbonate).
column4: Common around pans and fossil river valleys in the Kalahari, e.g. Makgadikgadi and Nxai Pan.
column5: Calcrete holds water near the surface, so pans and waterholes form on it.
column6: A white or cream crust under thin soil; often exposed on the edges of pans.
column7: Calcrete is used across Botswana as a cheap gravel for building roads.

column3: A banded form of quartz (chalcedony) that fills holes in volcanic rock.
column4: Botswana agate comes from the Bobonong area in the east, mainly sold as polished stones.
column5: Botswana agate is a well-known semi-precious stone used in jewellery.
column6: Look for smooth curved bands of colour, often pink, grey, brown and white.
column7: Each band of an agate was laid down as a separate layer of silica in a gas bubble.

column3: Four quartzite hills rising out of the flat Kalahari sand in north-west Botswana.
column4: Near Shakawe, west of the Okavango Panhandle.
column5: A UNESCO World Heritage Site with thousands of San and Bantu rock paintings.
column6: Name the four hills: Male, Female, Child and a small unnamed hill.
column7: The San call Tsodilo the "Mountains of the Gods" or "Rock that Whispers".

column3: Huge flat salt pans left behind when a giant ancient lake dried up.
column4: Central Botswana, between Maun and Nata; Nxai Pan is part of the same system.
column5: In good rains the pans fill and attract thousands of flamingos; zebra migrate here.
column6: Explain the super-lake of 200 000 km² that dried up about 10 000 years ago.
column7: The Makgadikgadi is one of the largest salt pan systems in the world.

column3: A granite rocky outcrop with baobabs, rising from the Sowa Pan in the Makgadikgadi.
column4: South-west part of Sowa Pan; reachable only in the dry season.
column5: A national monument and sacred site with stone walls and ancient shoreline features.
column6: Point out wave-cut terraces and fossil beach pebbles from the old lake shore.
column7: Kubu means "hippopotamus" in Setswana, from when the area was wet.

column3: Ridges of wind-blown sand; the Kalahari is the largest continuous body of sand in the world.
column4: Central and southern Kalahari; old fossil dunes are found under the bush in the north.
column5: The leached sand is poor in nutrients, so it has a low carrying capacity for herbivores.
column6: Red sand gets its colour from iron oxide coating the grains.
column7: Kalahari sand stretches from the Cape to the Congo.

column3: An inland delta where the Okavango River fans out over the Kalahari and never reaches the sea.
column4: North-west Botswana; best seen on a scenic flight, highest water June to August.
column5: Its floodplains are the most productive habitat in the Delta for wildlife.
column6: Explain the faults: Gumare fault spreads the water, Thamalakane fault blocks it in the south.
column7: The Delta drops only 60 m over 250 km; about 97% of the water is lost to evaporation and transpiration.

column3: Small tree-covered islands in the Delta, many started by termite mounds.
column4: All over the seasonal floodplains of the Okavango Delta.
column5: Islands give dry ground for trees, nesting birds and animals in the flood season.
column6: From the air: round islands with trees on the edges and a bare white salty centre.
column7: Many Delta islands began as a single termite mound that rose above the floodwater.

column3: A river that flows about 60 km along Botswana's northern border into the Zambezi.
column4: Chobe National Park riverfront near Kasane; best in the dry season, May to October.
column5: Huge herds of elephant and buffalo come to drink at the Chobe in the dry season.
column6: Tell guests it starts as the Kwando, becomes the Linyanti, then the Chobe.
column7: The Linyanti fault forces the Kwando's water north-east into the Chobe.

column3: A channel that links the Linyanti system to the Savuti Marsh; it flows and dries for years at a time.
column4: Savuti, in Chobe National Park, between Maun and Kasane.
column5: When it flows, the channel and marsh draw large numbers of game and predators.
column6: Dead trees along its banks grew while it was dry and drowned when the water returned.
column7: The channel stopped flowing in 1982 and only started again in 2008.

column3: The breaking down of rock where it lies, by heat, cold, water, plants and animals.
column4: Granite and sandstone outcrops in eastern Botswana and at the Tsodilo Hills.
column5: Weathering turns rock into soil, which decides which plants and animals live there.
column6: Point out rounded boulders peeling in layers like an onion from daily heating and cooling.
column7: Daily heating and cooling makes rock expand and shrink until it cracks.

column3: A partnership of a fungus and an alga that grows on bare rock.
column4: On rocks and old tree trunks; brightest after rain.
column5: Lichens slowly break rock down chemically and start the formation of soil.
column6: Explain the partnership: the fungus takes minerals from the rock and the alga makes food.
column7: Lichens cause chemical weathering: the fungus absorbs chemicals from the rock.

column3: Erosion is the removal of soil and rock particles by moving water or wind.
column4: Mainly south-eastern and eastern Botswana, where there is run-off; rare on flat Kalahari sand.
column5: Erosion moves soil away and starts the formation of new sedimentary rock.
column6: Gullies (dongas) form where water runs off bare, overgrazed ground.
column7: Flat, porous Kalahari sand soaks up rain, so most of Botswana shows little erosion.

column3: A national park famous for its huge elephant herds.
column4: Far north of Botswana, along the Chobe River near Kasane.
column5: Main attractions: the Chobe riverfront, Linyanti and Savuti.
column6: No off-road driving; summer gate times are 05:30-19:00.
column7: Mostly savanna, with large areas of miombo woodland in the north and east.

column3: A remote area of Chobe National Park with a marsh and a channel.
column4: South-western Chobe National Park, between Linyanti and Mababe.
column5: Known as one of the best areas in Africa for predators.
column6: The Savuti Channel dries up and flows again over many years.
column7: Savuti lions became famous for hunting elephants.

column3: A river and wetland area in the north-west of Chobe National Park.
column4: Along the Linyanti River on the Namibian border.
column5: Large elephant herds come to drink here in the dry season.
column6: The Kwando River is blocked by the Linyanti fault and turns north-east.
column7: Much of the area is private concession land with photographic lodges.

column3: A national park of open grassland and dry Kalahari savanna.
column4: North of the Makgadikgadi Pans, off the Maun-Nata road.
column5: Its waterhole is a wildlife hotspot in the hot, dry months.
column6: Most wildlife is on the grassy Nxai Pan, north of Baines' Baobabs.
column7: Zebra migrate between Nxai Pan and the Makgadikgadi Pans.

column3: A cluster of old baobab trees on a rocky ridge in Nxai Pan National Park.
column4: South of Nxai Pan, overlooking a salt pan and grassland.
column5: One of the most photographed landmarks in Botswana.
column6: Compare the trees with Baines' painting: they have changed very little.
column7: Thomas Baines painted these trees on an expedition in 1862.

column3: A national park established to protect the Sua and Ntwetwe salt pans.
column4: Central-northern Botswana, along the Boteti River.
column5: The Boteti River is a wildlife-rich area and a main attraction.
column6: In the dry season zebra and wildebeest crowd the Boteti to drink.
column7: The Boteti carries overflow from the Okavango towards Lake Xau.

column3: A game reserve set up to conserve the wildlife of the Okavango Delta.
column4: Eastern Okavango Delta, north of Maun.
column5: Public camps: South Gate, North Gate, Xakanaxa and Third Bridge.
column6: There is no vehicle access to Chief's Island; it has two lodges.
column7: Moremi was set up by the BaTawana people in 1963.

column3: About 52,800 km², one of Africa's largest reserves; established in 1961.
column4: In the heart of the Kalahari thirstland, central Botswana.
column5: Home to the San people and desert antelope like oryx, springbok and red hartebeest.
column6: Walking from lodge sites is allowed here; night drives are not.
column7: It is more than 1.5 times larger than Belgium.

column3: A community-run sanctuary declared to protect rhino.
column4: Near Serowe in the Central District.
column5: Breeds white and black rhino to restock Botswana's wild areas.
column6: In sanctuaries access times are flexible and night drives may be allowed.
column7: Killing a rhino can mean a P100 000 fine or 15 years in prison.

column3: A sanctuary established to protect flamingos.
column4: North-east corner of Sua Pan, near Nata village.
column5: One of only 5 breeding sites for lesser flamingo.
column6: As the last part of Sua Pan to dry up, it can give spectacular flamingo viewing.
column7: The fresh-to-salt water gradient gives good bird and plant diversity.

column3: Botswana's only transfrontier park, shared with South Africa.
column4: Far south-western Botswana, along the Nossob River.
column5: Red dunes and dry riverbeds hold gemsbok, springbok and black-maned lions.
column6: Look for game along the dry Nossob and Auob riverbeds.
column7: The planned KAZA area will be the world's largest transfrontier conservation area.

column3: Ancient rock paintings of animals, people and patterns.
column4: On the rock faces of the Tsodilo Hills.
column5: Shows thousands of years of human history and San beliefs.
column6: Never touch or wet the paintings; oil and water damage them.
column7: The main hills are called the Male, Female and Child.

column3: A huge inland delta; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014.
column4: North-western Botswana, fed by rivers from the Angolan highlands.
column5: Supports huge wildlife numbers, tourism and local people.
column6: The flood arrives in winter, months after the summer rains in Angola.
column7: It was the 1,000th site on the World Heritage list.

column3: One of the largest salt flats on Earth: Sua Pan and Ntwetwe Pan.
column4: North-eastern Botswana, between Nata, Gweta and Maun.
column5: A remnant of ancient Lake Makgadikgadi, which covered over 100,000 km².
column6: Ntwetwe Pan is more broken up and vegetated than Sua Pan.
column7: In good rains, thousands of flamingos come to the pans.

column3: A giant baobab named after the explorer James Chapman.
column4: Near Ntwetwe Pan, east of Makgadikgadi Pans National Park.
column5: An old landmark where early travellers left messages.
column6: It is on a private concession; visit from Jack's Camp or San Camp.
column7: The great tree collapsed in January 2016.

column3: A small game reserve declared to protect one species.
column4: At Otse, south of Gaborone.
column5: Protects a breeding colony of Cape griffon (Cape vulture) on the cliffs.
column6: All vultures are protected birds in Botswana.
column7: It shows that some reserves protect one species, not a whole wilderness.

column3: A town and the gateway to Chobe National Park.
column4: Far north-east Botswana, on the Chobe River.
column5: Close to Kazungula, where Botswana, Zambia, Zimbabwe and Namibia meet.
column6: Boat cruises on the Chobe River are the main activity.
column7: Victoria Falls is only about 80 km away.

column3: Botswana's tourism capital and gateway to the Okavango Delta.
column4: On the Thamalakane River at the south-eastern edge of the Delta.
column5: Most fly-in safaris to Delta camps start at Maun airport.
column6: Scenic flights from Maun show the Delta's channels and islands.
column7: The Thamalakane fault stops many Delta rivers near Maun.

column3: A trip in a mokoro, a dugout or fibreglass canoe pushed with a pole.
column4: Shallow channels of the Okavango Delta.
column5: Gives local polers income and a quiet, low-impact safari.
column6: In a storm, pole to shore as soon as possible.
column7: Mokoros were carved from big tree trunks; most are now fibreglass.

column3: Private game reserves in the Tuli Block, on freehold land.
column4: Eastern Botswana, where the Limpopo and Shashe rivers meet.
column5: Known for elephant, rocky koppies and big baobabs.
column6: Walks, horse rides and night drives are allowed on private land.
column7: Tuli is one of the few freehold land areas in Botswana.

column3: A shallow lake that fills and dries with the Okavango flood cycles.
column4: South-west of Maun, at the end of the Nhabe and Kunyere rivers.
column5: When full it attracts huge numbers of water birds.
column6: The Thaoge, its old main feeder, has not reached the lake in over 50 years.
column7: David Livingstone reached the lake in 1849.

column3: Low, puffy clouds with flat bases and rounded tops, like cotton wool.
column4: Common on summer mornings and afternoons across Botswana.
column5: Growing cumulus can build into thunderclouds by the afternoon.
column6: Cumulus means "heap" or "pile" in Latin.
column7: Fair-weather cumulus form as warm air rises off the ground and cools.

column3: A huge thundercloud that stretches from low level to the top of the sky, often with an anvil top.
column4: Summer afternoons (November to March), especially after hot, humid mornings.
column5: It brings lightning, heavy rain, strong wind and hail.
column6: Return to base at the first sign of thunderclouds, especially on a boat or on foot.
column7: Cumulonimbus is the only multi-level cloud: it covers all three cloud levels.

column3: A low, grey, even sheet of cloud near the ground, like high fog.
column4: Uncommon in Botswana; sometimes on cool, damp mornings during rainy spells.
column5: Stratus can bring drizzle but rarely heavy rain.
column6: Stratus means "sheet" in Latin.
column7: Stratus forms from 0 to 2 000 m and can touch the ground as fog.

column3: Low, lumpy grey and white clouds in a layer, with gaps of blue sky.
column4: Common in cooler months and after cold fronts.
column5: Usually only light rain or none; often breaks up during the day.
column6: Lumpy like cumulus but joined in a sheet like stratus; hence the name.
column7: Stratocumulus is the most common cloud type on Earth.

column3: A thick, dark grey rain cloud layer that hides the sun completely.
column4: In summer when the ITCZ brings rain for days at a time.
column5: Brings steady, long-lasting rain that soaks into the ground.
column6: Nimbus means "rain"; no shadows on the ground, and steady rain falling.
column7: Nimbostratus brings soft, steady rain rather than short storms.

column3: A grey or blue-grey sheet of middle-level cloud through which the sun looks watery.
column4: Often ahead of a summer rain front.
column5: It can thicken into nimbostratus and bring rain.
column6: The sun shines dimly "as through frosted glass" and casts no clear shadows.
column7: Alto means "high" but altostratus is a middle cloud, at 2 000 to 6 000 m.

column3: Middle-level clouds in white or grey patches or rolls, often in rows.
column4: Common across Botswana, especially in the morning in spring and summer.
column5: Altocumulus on a humid morning can mean afternoon thunderstorms.
column6: Hold up your hand: each cloudlet is about the size of a thumbnail (smaller for cirrocumulus).
column7: Rows of altocumulus are sometimes called a "mackerel sky".

column3: Thin, wispy high clouds made of ice crystals.
column4: Seen all year, especially in winter and before weather changes.
column5: Cirrus can be the first sign of an approaching front.
column6: Cirrus means "a curling lock of hair"; look for hooked, feathery streaks.
column7: Cirrus clouds float at 6 000 to 12 000 m where it is well below freezing.

column3: A thin, milky sheet of high ice cloud that covers the sky.
column4: Often ahead of a front; look around the sun or moon.
column5: It often comes before rain within a day or two.
column6: The best clue is a ring (halo) around the sun or moon.
column7: The ice crystals in cirrostratus bend the light to make the 22-degree halo.

column3: High clouds made of many tiny white ripples or grains, with no shadows.
column4: Not common and short-lived; seen in summer and spring.
column5: It shows moisture and instability high in the atmosphere.
column6: Like altocumulus but higher and smaller: each cloudlet is smaller than a fingertip.
column7: Cirrocumulus is one of the rarest of the ten main cloud types.

column3: A huge electric spark caused by an imbalance of charges, usually in a cumulonimbus.
column4: Summer thunderstorms, November to March.
column5: It forms nitric acid in the air, which fertilises the plants below.
column6: Count seconds from flash to thunder and divide by three to get the distance in km.
column7: Thunder is caused by the air expanding very fast as lightning super-heats it.

column3: A storm with lightning, thunder, strong wind and heavy rain from cumulonimbus clouds.
column4: Summer afternoons across Botswana, after hot, humid mornings.
column5: Storms bring most of Botswana's rain but can cause flash floods and falling trees.
column6: Never shelter under trees; mokoros should pole to shore; aluminium boats conduct lightning.
column7: Storms form as cold fronts replace the rising warm air in the afternoon.

column3: Balls or lumps of ice that fall from cumulonimbus storm clouds.
column4: Summer storms, especially with the unstable air of occluded fronts.
column5: Hail can damage crops, injure animals and strip leaves from trees.
column6: Hail plus cold wind after a storm can cause hypothermia; carry warm clothing.
column7: Never use alcohol to treat hypothermia; it lowers the core body temperature.

column3: An instrument with a funnel that collects rain in a cylinder to measure rainfall.
column4: At weather stations, camps and lodges; set in open ground.
column5: Rainfall figures show how much grazing and surface water the bush will have.
column6: It must be away from trees and buildings that could affect the reading.
column7: Kasane gets about 650 mm of rain a year, Ghanzi only about 430 mm.

column3: An instrument with spinning cups that measures wind speed.
column4: At airstrips and weather stations.
column5: Wind speed matters for flights, boat trips and fire risk.
column6: The ideal height is 10 m above open ground, away from trees and buildings.
column7: The faster the cups spin, the stronger the wind.

column3: A spinning column of rising hot air that picks up dust and leaves.
column4: Hot, still days in the dry season, especially August to October, on pans and open ground.
column5: Dust devils show strong heating of the ground, the same process that builds storm clouds.
column6: Unlike a tornado, a dust devil forms on a clear day and is not attached to a cloud.
column7: Dust devils can rise hundreds of metres but usually last only a few minutes.

column3: A wall of dust and sand carried by strong wind, often ahead of a storm.
column4: Late dry season (August to October) in the Kalahari and over the Makgadikgadi pans.
column5: Dust storms cut visibility and can ground flights and close roads.
column6: Close vehicle windows, protect cameras and keep guests' eyes covered.
column7: Dust from the Makgadikgadi pans can be seen from space.

column3: An arc of colours made when sunlight is bent and reflected by raindrops.
column4: After summer afternoon storms, with the sun low behind you.
column5: Rainbows often mean the storm is moving away.
column6: The sun is always behind you; red is on the outside of the main bow.
column7: In a double rainbow the colours of the second bow are reversed.

column3: Ice crystals that form on the ground and plants when the temperature drops below freezing.
column4: Winter mornings (June to August), especially in the Kalahari and low-lying areas.
column5: Frost kills tender plants and grass and can shape which trees grow in an area.
column6: Warn guests that early winter game drives can be below 0 °C; bring blankets.
column7: Ghanzi has recorded temperatures as low as -8.5 °C.

column3: An optical effect where hot air near the ground bends light, making "water" appear.
column4: Hot days on the Makgadikgadi pans, Nxai Pan and long straight roads.
column5: Mirages explain old travellers' stories of lakes that disappear.
column6: Distant trees or animals seem to float above a shimmering "lake".
column7: The "water" in a mirage is really an image of the sky.

column3: A ring of light around the sun or moon made by ice crystals in thin high cloud.
column4: When cirrostratus covers the sky, often before a change in weather.
column5: A halo is a traditional sign that rain may come within a day or two.
column6: The ring is about 22 degrees across: about the span of an outstretched hand.
column7: Halos are made by six-sided ice crystals bending light like tiny prisms.

column3: Tiny water droplets hanging in the air near the ground; cloud at ground level.
column4: Cold winter mornings over the Okavango, Chobe and Linyanti waterways.
column5: Morning mist over water is a beautiful photo opportunity on early boat trips.
column6: Mist forms when water is warmer than the cold air above it.
column7: Cold Benguela current air brings fog to the Namib coast but rarely reaches Botswana.
